title: The Lotus
hook: the Lotus of the True Law: a sutra of parables, visions and one great promise
carry: the lotus of the true law

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Diamond Sutra ended on its closing verse: look on the world like stars, like dew, like a bubble, like lightning. Your line: like dew, like lightning.

A lotus puts its roots down in pond mud, dark and soft. The stem climbs through murky water, and then, above the surface, the flower opens clean, as if it had never touched any of it. The Diamond Sutra was a blade: short, sharp, cutting away every grip. The next text on this path works in a different key. It tells stories. It stages visions the size of the sky. And it carries one promise so large that the people in the story don't believe it at first. It takes its name from that flower.
screen: `ROOTS IN THE MUD.` → `A FLOWER ABOVE THE WATER.` → `FROM A BLADE TO A STORY.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit the sutra is called the Saddharmapundarika. The scholar H. Kern, translating it into English, rendered the title as the Lotus of the True Law. Saddharma, the true Dharma, the true teaching. Pundarika, the lotus. So the title holds both the teaching and the flower. The image isn't new to this sutra. In a discourse in the Pali canon, the Buddha compares himself to a lotus: born in the water, grown up in the water, it rises above the water and stands unsoiled by it. So, he says, he was born and grew up in the world, yet lives unsoiled by it. Mud below, flower above, one plant. The Lotus is a sutra of parables. A father calling his children out of a burning house. A son who ran away and comes home not knowing he's the heir. A rain that falls on every kind of plant. A jewel sewn into a sleeping friend's robe. And it's a sutra of visions: a ray of light from the Buddha's brow, a jeweled stupa rising out of the earth, bodhisattvas springing up from the ground. Through it all runs one great claim: the Buddha's teachings, however many shapes they take, lead toward one goal, and those listening will themselves become Buddhas. Some East Asian schools, among them Tiantai in China and Tendai and Nichiren in Japan, place it at the center of their practice. On day one thousand you met Nichiren, for whom chanting the title itself is the practice. Over the coming weeks, this path walks through it story by story.
screen: `THE TEACHING AND THE FLOWER.` · `UNSOILED BY THE WATER.` · `PARABLES AND VISIONS.` · `ONE GREAT PROMISE.` · then, large: `THE LOTUS OF THE TRUE LAW.`

segments.voice: Let a few of the Lotus's pictures pass through your mind, one per breath: the burning house, the son who came home, the rain on all the plants, the jewel in the robe. Notice which one draws you, and stay with it, like a closed book with a good cover, waiting to be opened.
Saddharmapundarika. The Lotus Sutra's Sanskrit name: the lotus of the true Dharma, which Kern rendered the Lotus of the True Law. Today's word.
Your line: the lotus of the true law. The stories start tomorrow. Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

screen: `DAY 1150 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RAY OF LIGHT (KERN CH. 1).`

howItsDone: The Lotus Sutra is chanted, copied and studied in Mahayana communities in East Asia and beyond; Tiantai and Tendai Buddhists center their teaching on it, and in Nichiren Buddhism practitioners chant its title.

chat.says: Why is a Buddhist sutra named after a lotus, of all flowers?
options: The Buddha compared himself to a lotus: it grows up in the water yet stands above it, unsoiled.
Because the lotus only grows in India, where the Buddha taught, so it marks the place.
Because the lotus blooms just once, like a Buddha who appears only one time ever.
chat.meaning: In a Pali discourse the Buddha likens himself to a lotus that rises above the water unsoiled; the sutra's title joins that flower to the true teaching.
